# Dorfromantik (board game)
Dorfromantik: The Board Game (German: Dorfromantik – Das Brettspiel, lit. "village romance") is a 2022 cooperative tile-placement board game designed by Michael Palm and Lukas Zach, and published by Pegasus Spiele. It is an adaptation of the acclaimed 2021 video game Dorfromantik by Toukana Interactive. In the game, one to six players work together to place hexagonal landscape tiles and fulfill specific tasks in order to score points while building an idyllic countryside. The board game has no strict losing condition; players achieve a final score each session and can embark on a multi-session campaign to unlock additional content and challenges. Dorfromantik: The Board Game was highly praised and won the 2023 Spiel des Jahres (Game of the Year) award, marking the first time a video game adaptation has won that prestigious board game award.
## Gameplay
Dorfromantik: The Board Game is a fully cooperative, family-friendly tile-laying game. The components include a set of hexagonal landscape tiles showing different terrain types (such as forests, fields of grain, villages, railway tracks, and rivers) and a set of task tiles which indicate goals to achieve. At the start of each game, a few task tiles are placed face-up on the table; each task might require forming a contiguous area of a certain terrain type or other specific configurations (for example, connecting a cluster of forest tiles of a given size). On each turn, the active player draws and places a single tile, with the group collectively deciding how to position it. If fewer than three task tiles are currently in play, the player must draw a task tile to add a new goal; otherwise, they draw a landscape tile to extend the map. All tiles placed must adhere to simple placement rules – for instance, tracks and rivers cannot abruptly end against incompatible terrain types on adjacent tiles.
As the players expand the landscape, they aim to complete the task tiles’ requirements and create coherent features. Points are scored for each task tile fulfilled by the end of the game, as well as bonus points for other achievements: completing large areas marked with flag symbols and building the longest continuous railway line and the longest river on the board. The game continues until the supply of landscape tiles is exhausted. There is no way to lose; every game ends with a final score rather than a win/lose outcome. Players are encouraged to replay cooperatively to improve their high score.
A major feature of Dorfromantik: The Board Game is its campaign system. After each session, the collective score is recorded on a campaign progress track (often depicted as a meandering path on a campaign sheet). Reaching certain score thresholds allows the group to open one of five sealed boxes included in the game, each containing new game components such as additional tiles, new task cards, or other rule tweaks. These legacy-like elements gradually introduce fresh challenges and scoring opportunities, increasing the game’s complexity and difficulty over multiple plays. The campaign is replayable; the game can be reset so that new groups of players can start from the beginning, or players can choose to start over and explore different paths of unlocking content. A complete campaign yields a fully expanded set of tiles and tasks, but even after all content is unlocked the game remains playable as a high-score challenge with all components available.
The game supports 1 to 6 players (a solo mode is possible by a single player making all decisions) and is recommended for ages 8 and up. A typical session lasts around 30–60 minutes, though a full campaign spans several sessions. The cooperative nature of the gameplay means players discuss and plan moves together. The absence of any competitive element or timer gives Dorfromantik a relaxed, “zen” puzzle quality similar to its digital counterpart. Reviewers have noted that this calm, low-pressure experience makes the game inviting to a broad audience, including those new to board gaming or fans of the original video game.
## Development and release
The board game Dorfromantik was developed by Pegasus Spiele under license from Toukana Interactive, the creators of the PC video game. Michael Palm and Lukas Zach, a German board game design duo known for titles such as The Dwarves and Bang! The Dice Game, were responsible for translating the video game’s concept into a tabletop format. Notably, the video game’s original art style by illustrator Paul Riebe was retained in the board game, providing visual continuity between the two mediums. The designers and Toukana’s team opted to make the board game a cooperative experience in line with the video game’s laid-back, single-player nature, rather than introducing competitive mechanics. They also implemented a “resettable campaign” structure – drawing inspiration from the video game’s progression system of unlocking new tiles and biomes – to keep players engaged across multiple plays.
Pegasus Spiele officially announced Dorfromantik – The Board Game in mid-2022, describing it as a “zen” cooperative strategy puzzle and confirming it would feature a campaign with sealed content. The game debuted at the Essen Spiel trade fair in October 2022, where Pegasus released it to the public for the first time. It was made available in both German and English editions, among other languages, by Pegasus and its partners, with a recommended retail price around €35. The initial reception at Essen was positive, as many players noted the board game successfully captured the charm of the digital version’s peaceful landscape-building gameplay. By the end of 2022, Dorfromantik: The Board Game had begun appearing in retail stores in Europe and North America.
In developing the adaptation, Palm and Zach incorporated the core tile-placement mechanics of the video game (placing hexagonal pieces to form continuous terrains) and its scoring objectives, while simplifying certain aspects for tabletop play. For example, unlike the endless play of the video game, the board game uses a finite stack of tiles to impose a natural end to each session. Because players cannot earn additional tiles during play (whereas the video game awards extra tiles for completing tasks), the designers balanced the difficulty to ensure that most tasks can be completed within the fixed tile supply, and any remaining tasks simply go unfinished when the game ends. This design choice means that Dorfromantik on the tabletop becomes a relaxed optimization puzzle with no risk of failure – reinforcing the “feel-good” atmosphere emphasized by the Spiel des Jahres jury. The board game’s rulesheet credits the Toukana Interactive team for the original concept, but Palm and Zach are credited as the board game’s authors, reflecting their role in adapting the gameplay to a cooperative multiplayer format.
## Reception
Upon release, Dorfromantik: The Board Game received a warm critical response, and its popularity surged after it earned Germany’s Spiel des Jahres 2023 award (announced in July 2023). The Spiel des Jahres jury praised Dorfromantik as a “co-operative, feel-good game” that “takes the pressure out of everyday life”, noting that it provides new goals each play without ever pushing players out of their comfort zone. The jurors highlighted how even as tasks become slightly more challenging over time, the game remains gentle and relaxing, making it suitable for families and casual gamers. Dorfromantik’s win was historic for the award – it became the first board game based on a video game to be crowned Game of the Year, and also the first winner with legacy-style campaign elements (i.e. unlockable content) as part of its design. These milestones were seen as a sign of the board gaming hobby’s evolving scope, bringing in ideas from digital games and innovative mechanics in a genre traditionally dominated by standalone, non-digital designs.
Reviewers in the board gaming press have largely lauded Dorfromantik: The Board Game. Justin Bell of Meeple Mountain described it as a game that “combines an incredibly simple teach and infinite replayability”, thanks to its flexible modes (solo, multiplayer, one-off or campaign play) and gradually expanding content. He noted that the straightforward rules make it easy to introduce to new players, yet the scoring challenges and unlockables keep it engaging over many sessions. David W., writing for The Daily Worker Placement, declared Dorfromantik “one of the best ports of a videogame ever” in board game form, praising how it preserves the strategic puzzle feel of the digital version and delivers a smooth, accessible experience for a broad audience. He commended the high quality rulebook and components, and suggested the game has potential to attract video gamers into the board game hobby by virtue of its recognizable theme and cooperative play. Several outlets have also favorably compared Dorfromantik to the classic tile-layer Carcassonne, noting that both games involve building landscapes from tiles, though Dorfromantik is fully cooperative and focuses on collective high scores rather than competition.
Critics have offered a few caveats. Because the game is cooperative with open information, some groups might experience the “quarterbacking” or Pandemic effect – where one dominant player directs others’ moves in a collaborative game. The lack of a fail state means Dorfromantik is more of a relaxed activity than a tense game, which may not appeal to players seeking a challenge or direct player interaction. Nonetheless, most reviews regard these aspects as minor trade-offs for the intended calm tone of the game. By the end of 2023, Dorfromantik: The Board Game had become a commercial success in Europe, buoyed by the Spiel des Jahres win, and it introduced many new players to both tabletop gaming and the original video game. The game’s crossover success has been cited as an example of the growing synergy between video games and board games, as well as the continued popularity of cooperative and campaign-style board games.
## Expansions and spin-offs
Following the success of the base game, Pegasus Spiele and the designers expanded the Dorfromantik board game series with additional content and standalone titles. In August 2023, a small add-on titled The Great Mill (Die große Mühle) was released as a mini-expansion for Dorfromantik: The Board Game. It introduced an acrylic windmill figure and two new task cards, adding a minor gameplay element that can be mixed into the base game. Later in 2023, Pegasus launched Dorfromantik – The Duel, a standalone spin-off that reimagines the peaceful gameplay as a light competitive experience. Dorfromantik – The Duel is designed for two players (or two teams) who each use identical sets of tiles; on each turn both sides place the same tile simultaneously, striving to complete tasks and arrange their landscape more optimally than the opponent. Despite the head-to-head format, The Duel retains the core tile-placement and task completion concepts of the original, and even includes two new task types that can optionally be added into the cooperative base game.
In 2024, Pegasus Spiele released Dorfromantik – Sakura, a standalone cooperative sequel with a fresh theme inspired by Japanese scenery. Dorfromantik – Sakura applies the same fundamental mechanics of tile placement and campaign progression, but features new landscape elements like cherry blossom orchards, rice paddies, and stone pathways in place of the European countryside of the original game. The Sakura edition offers a new set of scenarios and tasks, demonstrating how the Dorfromantik system can be rethemed and expanded upon while maintaining its relaxing gameplay.
Continuing the line, in late 2025 Pegasus Spiele introduced Dorfromantik – Light Luggage, a travel-friendly version of the game packaged in a compact magnetic-clasp box. Light Luggage distills the cooperative campaign experience into a smaller format for one to four players, using scaled-down tiles and a high-score log in lieu of a sprawling campaign map. Players unlock new components by surpassing score thresholds, similar to the base game’s campaign, and the box even includes a few new materials that owners of the original board game can integrate as additional content. This portable edition aimed to make Dorfromantik more accessible for travel and quick play sessions, without losing the core charm of peaceful landscape building.
As of 2025, the Dorfromantik board game series encompasses the original cooperative board game and its mini-expansion, a two-player competitive variant, a sequel with a different setting, and a compact edition. The ongoing support and spin-offs underscore the game’s popularity and the versatility of its design in appealing to different audiences.

Dorfromantik – The Board Game awarded 2023 Spiel des Jahres
===========================================================

By[Nadine Pfaff](https://news.pegasus.de/en/author/nadine/)

![Image 9](https://news.pegasus.de/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/dorfromantik-game-of-the-year-announcement.webp)

**Pegasus Spiele is thrilled to share that Dorfromantik – The Board Game has been named Game of the Year 2023!**
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Friedberg, July 19, 2023: The Spiel des Jahres jury announced the annual winners for Kinderspiel (Children’s Game), Kennerspiel (Core Game) and Spiel des Jahres (Game of the Year) on Sunday evening. _[Dorfromantik – The Board Game](https://pegasusshop.de/en/Sortiment/Spiele/Familienspiele/15560/Dorfromantik-The-Boardgame)_ by Lukas Zach and Michael Palm, published by Pegasus Spiele, won over the jury and has been awarded the title 2023 Game of the Year.**

Pegasus Spiele is proud to have celebrated eight awards from the Spiel des Jahres jury between 2012 and 2022, most recently for _[Living Forest](https://pegasusshop.de/en/product-line/games/core-games/13509/living-forest-kennerspiel-des-jahres-2022)_, which won the Kennerspiel des Jahres 2022. In 2021, the jury awarded _[MicroMacro: Crime City](https://pegasusshop.de/en/product-line/games/family-games/11336/micromacro-crime-city)_ (with partner Edition Spielwiese) the Spiel des Jahres and _[Dragomino](https://pegasusshop.de/en/product-line/games/children-s-games/11649/dragomino-kinderspiel-des-jahres-2021)_ the Kinderspiel des Jahres. For 2023, Pegasus Spiele has secured the illustrious Spiel des Jahres again with _Dorfromantik – The Board Game._

_Dorfromantik_, the 2021 video game by Toukana Interactive, delighted the gaming community with its cute villages, burbling rivers, rustling forests, and wheat fields swaying in the wind. This peaceful building game inspired the core design of _Dorfromantik – The Board Game_ by Lukas Zach and Michael Palm, who delivered the experience to the tabletop in Autumn 2022.

In this fully cooperative tile placement game, one to six players work together to create an idyllic countryside that fulfills the wishes of the townspeople. Each player in turn will draw and place a single hexagonal tile, and the group is encouraged to work together towards achieving their goals. Ideal tile placement will score points for all completed tasks, in addition to the longest railway, the longest stream, and large enclosed areas of landscape marked by flags. At the end of each game, progress is marked along the meandering paths of a campaign tracker, which gradually unlocks additional tasks, unique tiles, and more game materials hidden in five sealed boxes. New challenges and clever scoring opportunities motivate players to explore all the different ways to increase one’s high score.

The Spiel des Jahres jury shared these thoughts about _Dorfromantik – The Board Game_:

> „_Dorfromantik_ takes the pressure out of everyday life. This co-operative, feel-good game presents new and exciting goals each time you play but there’s no danger of losing. Easily solved objectives are slowly replaced by trickier ones but nothing takes you out of your comfort zone. Working as a group to solve a puzzle means that everyone gets a chance to come up with the best idea. The campaign encourages you to play another game – and you can find new players in the time it takes to explain the rules.“

Wide landscapes in small format
-------------------------------

Latest game in the _Dorfromantik_ series published by Pegasus Spiele
--------------------------------------------------------------------

**Pegasus Spiele has released the next standalone game in the _Dorfromantik_ game series. [_Dorfromantik – Light Luggage_](https://pegasusna.com/Dorfromantik-Light-Luggage/PNA51245.USA "Dorfromantik – Light Luggage Product Page") packs the idyllic, cooperative core mechanics of Game of the Year 2023 [_Dorfromantik – The Board Game_](https://pegasusna.com/Dorfromantik-The-Boardgame/PNA51240.USA "Dorfromantik – The Board Game Product Page") into a portable magnetic box, with fresh gameplay to discover and achievements to unlock.**

_Dorfromantik – Light Luggage_ continues the successful tile-placement game series by designer duo Michael Palm & Lukas Zach, whose game idea is based on the video game of the same name by Toukana Interactive. The first board game in the series, _Dorfromantik – The Board Game_, was released at SPIEL Essen 2022 and was awarded Game of the Year in 2023. The goal of the game is easy to explain: one to six players aged eight and up work together to place hexagonal tiles to create an idyllic landscape, while trying to complete tasks to score points. Additionally, the longest train track, the longest river, and strategic placement of flags in completed areas will all contribute bonus points to the group’s final score. As players progress through the replayable campaign, they will unlock new components hidden in five secret boxes. These new game elements add additional challenges to the game that enable players to reach ever-higher scores,  every play.

In 2023, the competitive spin-off [_Dorfromantik – The Duel_](https://pegasusna.com/Dorfromantik-The-Duel-US-Edition/PNA51241.USA "Dorfromantik – The Duel Product Page") was released and transformed the popular feel-good title into a friendly competition. Two players, or two teams of players, aged eight and up use identical tiles each turn to try and fulfil the village's tasks to score more points than their opponent. [_Dorfromantik – Sakura_](https://pegasusna.com/Dorfromantik-Sakura/PNA51243.USA "Dorfromantik – Sakura Product Page"), a standalone cooperative sequel with a beautiful Japanese aesthetic, was released in 2024 and invited players to design a countryside dotted with cherry blossoms, rice paddies, and meandering stone paths.

_Dorfromantik – Light Luggage_ introduces a brand-new cooperative campaign for one to four players aged 8 and up and is, once again, illustrated by Paul Riebe. The box is only a quarter of the size of its predecessors and the tiles are smaller, requiring less space. This is ideal for anyone who is traveling, playing on small gaming tables, or looking for a compact introduction to the _Dorfromantik_ experience that is perfect for a midday break.

Even in this handy size, the cozy atmosphere of the series remains intact: long rivers, flags in completed areas, and fulfilled tasks from the residents earn points at final scoring. Packaged in a practical magnetic box, players of _Dorfromantik – Light Luggage_ will track their high score each game, instead of progressing along a campaign map. By exceeding each scoring threshold on the high score track, players will unlock new components and challenges for their next session. The compact box also includes new material for owners of _Dorfromantik – The Board Game_.

Dorfromantik: The Board Game Review
===================================

So peaceful
-----------

October 18, 2023

[Justin Bell](https://www.meeplemountain.com/authors/justin-bell/)

5 Min Read

  

[More Board Game Reviews](https://www.meeplemountain.com/reviews/)

Dorfromantik is now both a video game and a board game! Find out what Justin thinks about the 2023 Spiel des Jahres winner in his review.

[Dorfromantik - The Boardgame](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0BQ3W9GRL?tag=meeplmount-20&linkCode=ogi&th=1&psc=1)

When a game wins a major tabletop award before you review it, you don’t really have much ground to stand on.

The world already agrees that _Dorfromantik: The Board Game_ (2022, [Pegasus Spiele](https://www.meeplemountain.com/publishers/pegasus-spiele/)) is at least a very good game, because it won the prestigious [Spiel des Jahres](https://boardgamegeek.com/awardset/80324/2023-spiel-des-jahres) over the summer.

While there’s always commentary on the games that win this award (in part because there’s always a debate on the shifting sands around the weight of games in this category), time is usually kind to the winners. If you look at the list of winners since [_CATAN_](https://www.meeplemountain.com/articles/games-we-love-catan/) won in 1995, almost every single one is still being celebrated today. This year alone, I’ve been at game nights where we played _Just One, Codenames,_ [_Pictures_](https://www.meeplemountain.com/reviews/pictures/), [_Dominion_](https://www.meeplemountain.com/reviews/dominion/), [_Hanabi_](https://www.meeplemountain.com/reviews/hanabi/), [_Azul_](https://www.meeplemountain.com/reviews/azul/), and [_Kingdomino_](https://www.meeplemountain.com/reviews/kingdomino/). Many of these made repeat appearances.

Those are all amazing games. _Dorfromantik: The Board Game_ is no different. That’s because it combines an incredibly simple teach and infinite replayability in a package that can be played solo, multiplayer, campaign-style, and/or as a high-score challenge.

I get it now. _Dorfromantik_ is really good.

![Image 7](https://b1803394.smushcdn.com/1803394/wp-content/uploads/2023/10/Dorfromantik-1-1024x768.jpg?lossy=1&strip=1&webp=1)

Spelling Error
--------------

_Dorfromantik_ is a cooperative tile-laying game for 1-6 players, although given the ruleset, I decided to just play this solo.

A series of Task tiles are laid out on the table, face down. These Tasks drive the action of _Dorfromantik_ by asking players to complete, well, tasks—lay five tiles with forest scenery adjacent to at least one edge of another tile featuring forest scenery, for example. To begin the game, three of those Task tiles are placed, adjacent to another Task tile on at least one edge. Then players can either place a Landscape tile, or place another Task tile if there are ever less than three Tasks currently in play.

The landscapes (all of which are shuffled and placed face-down in stacks during setup) come in five flavors: forests, grain, villages, tracks, and streams. Tracks and streams have more rules than the other three terrain types, in that they just can’t run into other terrain types without continuing as tracks or streams. (This becomes obvious when you see the game on the table; who would construct an area where a stream just dead-ends in a village?)

So, turns are simple. Place a tile, try to complete a Task, place more tiles. Each time I sat down to play _Dorfromantik_, I was slowly entranced by the way action plays out. It’s a peaceful puzzle, one that allows for clever play by setting up not only your current Tasks, but your future ones too. In the base game, you have 25 total Task tiles, and five of each of the five terrain types. I regularly found myself flipping tiles and setting up a future where I could knock out a five-tile grain Task, for example, by creating a small section of three or four grain tiles that created a contiguous grain section.

The game ends when you run out of landscape tiles and need to place one. Scores are tallied, with the majority of your score in the base game tied to the total value of the tasks completed. If you wanted to just play a single game, that’s that. You “win” every time you play _Dorfromantik_, but you’re encouraged to play a campaign, and that’s where _Dorfromantik_ really shines: unlockables, and additional ways to give life to extended plays.

![Image 8](https://b1803394.smushcdn.com/1803394/wp-content/uploads/2023/10/Dorfromantik-2-768x1024.jpg?lossy=1&strip=1&webp=1)

It’s the Unlocks, Stupid
------------------------

_Dorfromantik_ is a pleasant time at the table, to use a word my colleague [Andrew Lynch](https://www.meeplemountain.com/authors/andrew-lynch/) employs from time to time. I wasn’t wowed by the initial experience, but I admit that it was pleasant to sit at my kitchen table with a glass of wine and listen to classical music in the background.

But if you play _Dorfromantik_ as a campaign game, you add up your scores and log them on a campaign sheet. As you slowly work your way up the cumulative scoring track, you’ll unlock up to five small boxes’ worth of extras. This extra stuff provides a number of different ways to play, challenges to achieve, scoring boosts, and other odds and ends.

In this way, _Dorfromantik_ is like many of the “roguelite” video games I play on my Xbox. You play for 15-20 minutes, die a horrible death (only in those video games…you don’t die in _Dorfromantik_!!), unlock a new skin / power / weapon that grants different playstyles for the next run. And that’s how designers Michael Palm and Lukas Zach get their hooks into you with _Dorfromantik_.

![Image 9](https://b1803394.smushcdn.com/1803394/wp-content/uploads/2023/10/Dorfromantik-3-1024x768.jpg?lossy=1&strip=1&webp=1)

During the campaign, you unlock another piece of content every game or two. And you want to get to the end of that campaign sheet, so you think “let me just play one more round tonight” and that turns into another round.

Or four.

_Dorfromantik_ achieves something that not many board games do—create a real hook to play the game over and over again, right away. You can always get a little better each time you play. _Dorfromantik_’s games have usually played out in about 20-25 minutes as a solo game, a little longer if I am deliberate in my approach. At least in the first playthrough, there’s always another small piece of content that required my attention or needed an unlock. Or there’s a challenge that can be completed if I just work a little harder.

You get the idea. I don’t expect to come back to _Dorfromantik_ now that I’ve finished up my review plays, mainly because high-score challenges aren’t my cup of tea. But even as a non-believer, the design here is excellent and the system creates such a great reason to keep coming back.

Well played, _Dorfromantik_. Now I might have to check out the video game to see what I’ve been missing!

##### AUTHOR RATING

*   Great - Would recommend.

A Dorfromantik board game is on the way, and it's due to launch toward the end of 2022.

Developed by industry mainstay Pegasus Games, the Dorfromantik board game - which is inspired by Toukana Interactive's [zen strategy puzzle game](https://www.gamesradar.com/have-you-tried-a-city-builder-without-the-chaos-of-well-cities-in-dorfromantik/) on Steam - is a co-op tile-laying challenge where players build "idyllic village landscapes, immersing themselves in a calm, peaceful world" according to the [official press release](https://pegasus.de/presse/pressemitteilungen/wunderbare-landidylle). Although we don't yet have a firm release date, it should join other strategy [board games](https://www.gamesradar.com/best-board-games/) in stores "in the 4th quarter of 2022 with a recommended retail price of €34.99".

This tabletop version of Dorfromantik (which translates to 'Village Romance') seems to take a lot of inspiration from [classic board games](https://www.gamesradar.com/best-board-games/) like Carcassonne, wherein players lay down tiles to form a board of landscapes to gain points. Here, up to six people will put down a variety of hexagonal tiles to "fulfill the orders of the population". It seems that you'll get points for creating the longest track or river as well as for flag tokens in completed areas. Additionally, new tiles are unlocked over time with fresh challenges that allow you to increase your high score. These tiles are kept secret until you need them via sealed boxes, and although they increase the game's difficulty, "players can always start over and try out new paths" due to what Pegasus Games calls a 'campaign block'.

The Dorfromantik board game is estimated to last between 30 and 60 minutes.

This isn't the first time a relaxing video game has made its way to tabletop, of course; a [Stardew Valley board game](https://www.gamesradar.com/stardew-valley-board-game-back-on-sale-with-revised-cards-and-rules/) is also on shelves now, and it's one of the more chilled-out [board games for families](https://www.gamesradar.com/board-games-for-families/) out there. However, we shouldn't need to worry too much about this one selling out so fast. Because Dorfromantik is being distributed by tabletop powerhouse Pegasus Games, it be should be fairly easy to get hold of as and when it hits shelves.

Germany’s prestigious Spiel des Jahres award goes to Dorfromantik: The Board Game. Here’s a full rundown of the winner and the runner ups from Spiel des Jahres 2023

It was a big night for game designers across the world on Sunday 16th, as many designers, publishers and press were present at the nhow Berlin conference centre to find out who was the winners of [the _Spiel Des Jahres 2023_ awards](https://www.spiel-des-jahres.de/en/award-winners-2023/).

If you’re new here, the Spiel des Jahres (Game of the Year) is, of course, a prestigious award for board and card games, first created back in 1978 with the purpose of rewarding family-friendly game design, and promoting excellent games. Though it started predominately to celebrate games within the German market, it has since grown and is recognised as an achievement across the tabletop gaming community internationally.

![Image 1: Spiel des Jahres 2023 game of the year](https://azure.wgp-cdn.co.uk/app-table-top-gaming/posts/Spiel-des-Jahresgameoftheyeartabletopgaming.jpg)

After a moving opening video celebrating the life of _Catan_ designer Klaus Teuber, it was announced that the _Kinderspiel_ (or children’s game) winner this year was spooky mystery co-op _Mysterium: Kids_, _Kennerspiel_ (hobbyist game) winner was card battling delight _Challengers!_ And the final and biggest award, the ‘Game of the Year’ 2023 went to the charming village builder _Dorfromantik: The Board Game._

This win marks two firsts for a _Spiel Des Jahres_ winner: the first winner which was an adaptation of a video game as well as the first winner which also has legacy components that add new elements to the game which offer new challenges. As a lot of pundits around the world have spoken out about the relevancy of this award in modern board game culture, it’s interesting to see this year’s big winner not only including one of the more revelatory new mechanics in board games, but also an idea that has come from outside of tabletop gaming, showing the broadening cultural connection that tabletop games are now offering to players across the world.

The night also saw a special award given to game series _Unlock!_ For its contributions to exploring new fields of tabletop gaming with its series of co-operative ‘Escape the Room’ style games.

### [Dorfromantik: The Board Game wins 2022 Spiel des Jahres](https://dailyworkerplacement.com/2023/07/25/dorfromantik-the-board-game-wins-2022-spiel-des-jahres/)

by | published Tuesday, July 25, 2023

[![Image 1](https://dailyworkerplacement.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/07/featured-1520x1140.jpg)](https://dailyworkerplacement.com/2023/07/25/dorfromantik-the-board-game-wins-2022-spiel-des-jahres/)

[Dorfromantik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorfromantik) was one of the sleeper videogame hits of COVID-19. Released on March 21, 2021, its contemplative, puzzly tile-laying gameplay was complemented totally by its super-chill soundtrack (composed by Laryssa Okada and Pygoscelis and tonally very much in the vein of [Jose Gonzalez](https://www.google.com/search?gs_ssp=eJzj4tTP1Tcwr8wzzjBg9OLNyi9OVUjPz6tKzEmtAgBoygiL&q=jose+gonzalez&rlz=1C1CHBF_enCA1023CA1023&oq=jose+gonzalez&aqs=chrome.1.0i355i433i512j46i433i512j0i512j46i512l3j0i512l4.3504j0j4&sourceid=chrome&ie=UTF-8)’s solo acoustic albums). I first heard about it when one of my favorite YouTubers ([ManyATrueNerd](https://www.youtube.com/@ManyATrueNerd)) and his wife both became obsessed with it, livestreaming head-to-head challenges and getting into deep discussions about gameplay.

For me (along with many in the tabletop world, I assume), **Dorfromantik**’s success was welcome and highly amusing. For what was **Dorfromantik** at heart but a tweaked version of [Carcassonne](https://boardgamegeek.com/boardgame/822/carcassonne)? Solo mode only, hex instead of square tiles, and meeples replaced by terrain-completion objectives, and you could keep the game going forever, in theory, if you kept gaining extra tiles by achieving those objectives.

But I’m not knocking **Dorfromantik**–not at all! According to Steam I’ve spent almost 150 hours playing it–much more than any digital port of **Carcassonne**–so I must like it. If anything, it shows how presentation and immersion make all the difference. The little animations on the tiles, the streamlined yet strategic gameplay, and the hypnotic soundtrack all work in **Dorf**’s favour.

Its popularity began to spread through my tabletop friend network. People started posting screenshots of high scores and HUGE layouts of completed games. I wondered if and when **Dorf** would be licensed for actual physical tabletop play, and if so what that would look like.

[I’ve written before](https://dailyworkerplacement.com/2021/02/26/from-screen-to-tabletop-five-great-boardgame-versions-of-video-games/) about the possible perils of porting from videogames to tabletop and _vice versa_. Gameplay, components (and fiddliness thereof), and player interaction rarely translate from one media to the other without considerable adaptation.

Yet with **Dorf** we had a videogame that felt, for all intents, like a boardgame–yet it was not. That made it a slam-dunk in terms of translating from digital to analog–or did it? So when PegasusSpiele released [Dorfromantik: The Board Game](https://boardgamegeek.com/boardgame/370591/dorfromantik-board-game) in late 2022, the natural question was: slam-dunk or air-ball?

![Image 2: Top-down shot of Dorfromantik: The Board Game against a tourquoise background.](https://dailyworkerplacement.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/07/dorfcover-1566x1140.jpg)

The verdict is now in: **Dorfromantik: The Board Game** just won the coveted _Spiel des Jahres_ for Game of the Year for 2022. So clearly lots of people–lots of _German_ people anyway–felt the boardgame succeeded. Let’s look at why that might be so.

I don’t know how much say the **Dorf** videogame dev team had in the boardgame. They are credited on the last page of the rules along with Lukas Zach and Michael Palm, as well as the illustrator of both versions Paul Riebe (good call there, btw; changing art styles would have been way too jolting). But only Zach and Palm are the only ones credited on BGG. They’ve been collaborating for about ten years; their first hit together was 2012’s [The Dwarves](https://boardgamegeek.com/boardgame/124668/dwarves) followed soon after by 2013’s [Bang! The Dice Game](https://boardgamegeek.com/boardgame/143741/bang-dice-game).

Either way someone had to decide whether the tabletop version should be competitive or co-operative (or include both as options). Each mode has things going for it. In the end, **Dorf: TBG** is co-operative, and I think that was the right choice, being more in the contemplative spirit of the original.

Similarly, I don’t know whose idea it was to make the game into a resettable campaign–but once again I applaud. It flows naturally from the way different types of tiles are unlocked in the original, and also translates achievement-unlocking in a seamless way. The circuitous paths of the Campaign Sheet mean that you can make different choices each time you play a campaign.

Gameplay itself is only slightly more complex than the videogame version: on your turn you either reveal and play a Task tile (if fewer than 3 are in play) or a Landscape tile. Task tiles set goals for contiguous groups of terrain; hexagonal Landscape tiles add to the terrain. The goal is to complete as many tasks as possible before the Landscape tiles run out. Unlike the videogame, you can’t earn bonus tiles for completing Tasks–but you will earn bonus VP at the end of the game for building certain configurations of tiles and tile features which unlock as the campaign progresses.

![Image 3: Campaign sheet for Dorfromantik: The Board Game, showing VP thresholds, achievement list, and unlocking path.](https://dailyworkerplacement.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/07/dorftsheet-1-1424x1140.jpg)

Now, I don’t always agree with the games that are nominated or crowned at the _Spiel des Jahres_. 2021’s [MicroMacro: Crime City](https://boardgamegeek.com/boardgame/318977/micromacro-crime-city) was a fine game-slash-activity, but in a year that saw the incredible innovations of both [The Initiative](https://boardgamegeek.com/boardgame/328908/initiative) and [That Time You Killed Me](https://boardgamegeek.com/boardgame/344258/time-you-killed-me) it was a lost opportunity.

BUT, in the case of **Dorf: TBG** I think the _Spiel_ jury picked right. **Dorfromantik** is one of the best ports of a videogame ever, and therefore has the potential to reach a huge audience and expand the hobby. Its gameplay is straightforward but not simplistic. And its presentation, right down to its excellent rules (not a single error or ambiguity, sadly rare today) guarantees a smooth onboarding for both n00bs and veterans. Being fully cooperative and with no mechanic to prevent [the Pandemic Effect](https://dailyworkerplacement.com/2019/03/11/5-co-op-games-that-avoid-the-pandemic-effect/) is a strike against it, at least for some. But if you are looking for a game to introduce someone to the hobby, especially a videogamer who loves the original, you can’t do better than **Dorfromantik**…at least, not until the [Slay the Spire](https://boardgamegeek.com/boardgame/338960/slay-spire-board-game) boardgame comes out later in the year (🤞🏻).
